policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Japan's comprehensive national 'AI Strategy 2022', decided by the Integrated Innovation Strategy Promotion Council on April 22, 2022 (Reiwa 4), expanding AI Strategy 2019 and 2021 in response to COVID-19, mega-disaster risks, climate departure, and geopolitical shifts (subsequently superseded by the December 2025 First AI Basic Plan). Structured in four parts: Part 1 establishes Strategic Goals 0–4 (imminent crisis resilience, AI talent, real-world industrial competitiveness, inclusive sustainable society, and global research/education networks); Part 2 details 'AI for National Resilience' (disaster/armed-attack Digital Twins, global BCP/data-economy networks), 'AI for Planetary Resilience' (Nature-Positive Economy), and 'Resilient and Responsible AI' (XAI, Federated Learning, Security for AI / AI for Security); Part 3 promotes social implementation (human-AI collaboration, breaking black-box fears, physical-cyber 'Round 2 of DX', data-handling rule reviews, government adoption, and focusing on Japanese strengths); Part 4 sets 2025 education targets (1M high school grads, 500k university/KOSEN grads, 250k applied AI talent, 2,000 experts, 1M working adults/yr recurrent education), R&D network restructuring, trust-data infrastructure, Digital Government AI guidelines, SME/startup support, and international ethics/standardization (GPAI presidency) avoiding excessive regulatory constraints.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: Economic competitiveness is the dominant frame of AI Strategy 2022: it casts international competitiveness as a matter of 'Japan's survival' (Strategic Goals 1–4), warns that Japan lost 'Round 1' of cyberspace DX to the US and risks falling permanently behind US and Chinese tech giants, charts a 'winning path' in physical-cyber 'Round 2 of DX' and real-world industries to close Japan's labor-productivity gap, boosts SMEs and startups, and explicitly reframes even Strategic Goal 0's crisis resilience into business-creation and industrial-competitiveness policy. Innovation enablement is a strong runner-up, driving Society 5.0 adoption, removing institutional barriers, building Responsible AI/XAI to dispel black-box hesitation, accelerating Digital Government uptake, and engaging international standards to prevent excessive regulatory constraints. Consumer and public safety is a prominent third frame centered on Part 2's Strategic Goal 0—protecting citizens' lives and property from pandemics, mega-earthquakes, floods, climate threats, and cyber/data-poisoning vulnerabilities. Labor transition (recasting AI as human-collaborative rather than job-replacing and scaling recurrent education to 1 million working adults per year), national security (economic security, geopolitical contingencies, armed-attack civilian protection, tech-outflow rules, cybersecurity hardening), and fundamental rights (Human-Centric AI principles, bias/privacy safeguards, government fairness/transparency) appear as substantive supporting frames.

セスともいうべきＤＸにおいては、米国が大きく成長している反面、日本は世界的競争の
中で優位を占めることができなかった。今後、現実空間（フィジカル空間）とサイバー空
間の融合領域に主戦場が移り、ＤＸの二回戦ともいうべき状況に差し掛かってくる。日本
がフィジカル空間での強みを生かしたＡＩの実装を進め、社会を変革することで、「勝ち

evidence_spans.source_section: 第三部 １．社会実装をめぐる背景 (Page 23)
evidence_spans.quote_en: In DX—the pioneering of cyberspace thus far—the US grew strongly while Japan failed to gain an advantage in global competition. Going forward, the main battleground shifts to the fusion of physical space and cyberspace ('Round 2 of DX'), where Japan can find its 'winning path' by leveraging its physical-space strengths to implement AI and transform society.

evidence_spans.quote_en: Meanwhile, Strategic Goals 1–4 form the foundation of Japan's sustainable industry and society, requiring sustained and steady action with Japan's survival at stake to maintain international competitiveness.
